content: The successful transition from parenteral nutrition to full enteral feeding in the neonatal period is crucial for promoting growth in preterm infants. Lactase, an enzyme responsible for breaking down lactose, is the last major intestinal disaccharidase to develop in preterm infants. Due to insufficient lactase activity, preterm infants are unable to properly digest lactose. Lactase preparations may be used to hydrolyze lactose in formula or breast milk, potentially reducing lactose malabsorption in these infants. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of adding lactase to milk, compared to a placebo or no intervention, in promoting growth and feeding tolerance in preterm infants. The primary outcomes assessed included weight gain (measured in grams per kilogram per day), growth metrics (weight, length, and head circumference percentiles for postmenstrual age), and the number of days required to achieve full enteral feeding. Secondary outcomes included common complications associated with preterm birth and any adverse effects. Searches for relevant studies were conducted electronically and manually in January 2005 and repeated in May 2012. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, along with abstracts from Pediatric Academic Societies' and European Society of Pediatric Research meetings. The Web of Science was also searched, starting with a previously identified trial by Erasmus in 2002, to locate additional studies citing this trial. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving preterm infants born at less than 37 weeks postmenstrual age. The intervention of interest was the addition of lactase to milk, compared to a placebo or no intervention. Data collection and analysis followed the standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Treatment effects were calculated using risk ratio (RR), risk difference (RD), and mean difference (MD), all with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A fixed-effect model was used for meta-analyses, but heterogeneity tests were not performed as only one study met the inclusion criteria. The updated search in May 2012 did not identify any additional studies. The single included study was a high-quality, double-blind, randomized controlled trial involving 130 preterm infants born between 26 and 34 weeks postmenstrual age, with a mean postnatal age of 11 days at enrollment. Lactase-treated feeds were initiated when enteral feedings accounted for more than 75% of daily intake. However, none of the primary outcomes outlined in the review protocol were reported in this study. Among the secondary outcomes, only necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) was reported. The risk ratio for NEC was 0.32 (95% CI 0.01 to 7.79), and the risk difference was -0.02 (95% CI -0.06 to 0.03), indicating a reduction that was not statistically significant. The study found a statistically significant increase in weight gain at day 10 in the group receiving lactase-treated feeds, but this effect was not observed at other time points. Overall, there was no statistically significant effect on weight gain. Importantly, no adverse effects were reported in the study. The authors concluded that the single randomized trial available to date does not provide evidence of significant benefits from adding lactase to feeds for preterm infants. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of this intervention before it can be recommended for clinical practice. Future randomized controlled trials should compare lactase-treated feeds to placebo and enroll infants at the time enteral feeding is introduced. These trials should assess the primary and secondary outcomes for effectiveness and safety as outlined in this review.
